query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy, the targeted addition of a refractory element (tungsten) will improve high-temperature mechanical properties relative to the alloy without tungsten.
generation.material_initial_state: A HEA with titanium and nickel as primary constituents that meets the definition (each element at 5–35 at%)
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 10 atomic % tungsten by reducing the atomic percentages of other elements proportionally to maintain an overall HEA composition.
generation.conditions: Testing under elevated temperatures (800–1000°C) and under constant load environments typical for creep and high-temperature strength assessments.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced lattice distortion and possible formation of stable nano-precipitates in the tungsten-added alloy.
generation.mechanism: The tungsten addition increases lattice distortion leading to solid-solution strengthening, and it may also facilitate the formation of stable secondary phases that hinder dislocation motion and slow creep at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The tungsten-enhanced alloy is expected to show a significant improvement (e.g., ≥15% increase) in yield strength and a marked reduction in creep rate relative to the baseline alloy without tungsten.
generation.baseline: Titanium- and nickel-primary HEA without tungsten addition, processed under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: The intervention applies within operating temperatures of 800–1000°C and within the compositional limits of high-entropy alloys (5–35 at% per element), using standard processing routes for HEAs.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvement and the detailed nature of precipitate phases are uncertain, as microstructural evolution might vary with minor compositional or processing differences.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one set is the base titanium- and nickel-primary HEA and the other set includes ~10 at% tungsten addition, adjusted to keep overall alloy composition within HEA boundaries. Subject both sets to identical thermal and mechanical processing.
measurements: High-temperature yield strength measured at 800, 900, and 1000°C
Creep rate under constant load at these temperatures
Microstructural characterization (via SEM/TEM) to detect precipitate formation and lattice distortion
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-added alloy does not demonstrate at least a 15% improvement in yield strength or fails to show a statistically significant reduction in creep rate compared to the baseline HEA, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

chosen.approach: Targeted element additions to enhance HEA high-temperature properties
